![[5zfymn6nqr7n7dg3vv77ngbr15]]

This is what I called the "liveness" problem in a substack note at one point, that I'll find and append here later. But the tldr is that generated text is anaerobic. It does not "breathe" live information the way human generated text does. We are not frozen archival models with some "fine tuning" and "RAG" bolted on. We are more like continuous integration engines that constantly weave together information retrieved from long-term memory with information buffering in short-term memory.

One fun exercise to understand this phenomenon is to try and write something based entirely on stuff that's long over in your life but has little to no emotional salience (ie, it's not still part of your "living" persona where you're still processing the meaning). Like, try to reconstruct a boring vacation from 10 years ago based on photos and emails from that time. You'll end up with a similarly dead, tiring feel to the writing.

One of the goals of blygger is in fact to solve that very problem. That's why the \[\[TK\]\] mechanism exists -- to interleave generated and human in a hopefully more live way. But the deeper solution is to run generation on live stream contexts somehow.

Like, try to reconstruct a boring vacation from 10 years ago based on photos and emails from that time. You'll end up with a similarly dead, tiring feel to the writing.
